title: Revision notes
basis: Condensed exam notes covering every concept in your CISA revision material (Domains 1-5) plus the 28th edition CRM Domain 4 changes, rewritten in short exam-ready points and mapped to the current syllabus topics.

outdated.now: Current outline (Aug 2024): D1 18%, D2 18%, D3 12%, D4 26%, D5 26%.
COBIT 2019 is the current framework (governance system, design factors, focus areas).
BIA, BCP, DRP and backups now sit in Domain 4B (Business Resilience).
New 4.9 in the 28th edition CRM (topic 4A9) - added below.
4.5 Shadow IT and EUC is emphasised in the new syllabus (topic 4A5) - added below.

cards.title: Audit charter
points: Formal document giving the audit function its purpose, authority, responsibility and accountability.
Approved by the audit committee or the board (the most senior governing body), not by IT or line management.
Gives auditors unrestricted access to records, people and systems needed for the work.
Changes rarely; the annual audit plan changes every year.
cards.tip: If asked who approves the charter, pick the most senior governance body offered (audit committee / board).

cards.title: Independence and professional ethics
points: Auditors must be independent in fact and in appearance; report functionally to the audit committee.
Do not audit work you designed, implemented or operated; disclose any impairment.
ISACA Code of Professional Ethics: due care, objectivity, confidentiality, competence, support standards.
The auditor recommends; management decides and implements.
cards.tip: Answers where the auditor fixes, approves or implements controls are almost always wrong.

cards.title: ISACA ITAF: standards, guidelines, tools
points: Standards are mandatory; guidelines explain how to apply them; tools and techniques are examples.
General standards (independence, proficiency), performance standards (planning, evidence, sampling) and reporting standards.
cards.tip: Mandatory = standards. Everything else supports them.

cards.title: Types of audits
points: Compliance, financial, operational, integrated, administrative, IS, specialized (e.g. third-party / SOC reports) and forensic audits.
Forensic audits gather evidence for investigation of fraud or crime and must preserve chain of custody.
Relying on other auditors or experts requires assessing their competence, independence and work quality.

cards.title: Audit planning steps
points: Understand the business, its objectives, processes and the IT that supports them.
Identify laws and regulations, perform a risk assessment, then set scope and objectives.
Build the audit program: procedures, resources, timing and evidence needed.
Long-term (annual) plans are risk-based and reviewed by the audit committee.
cards.tip: The FIRST step in planning is understanding the business and its objectives.

cards.title: Risk analysis and risk-based audit
points: Risk = likelihood x impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability against an asset.
Risk-based auditing focuses effort on areas of highest risk, so audit resources give the most assurance.
Audit risk = inherent risk x control risk x detection risk; the auditor can only influence detection risk.
Inherent risk exists before controls; control risk is that controls fail to prevent/detect; detection risk is that the auditor misses an error.
cards.tip: When resources are limited, audit the highest-risk areas first.

cards.title: Risk treatment options
points: Mitigate (reduce with controls), transfer/share (insurance, outsourcing), avoid (stop the activity), accept (within appetite).
Risk acceptance must be a documented decision by an authorized owner, not by the auditor.
Residual risk is what remains after treatment and should be within risk appetite.
cards.tip: Transferring risk moves the financial impact, not accountability.

cards.title: Internal controls: preventive, detective, corrective
points: Preventive controls stop problems before they occur (segregation of duties, access controls, input validation).
Detective controls find problems after they occur (logs review, reconciliations, hash totals, IDS).
Corrective controls reduce impact and restore (backups, BCP/DRP, incident procedures).
Compensating controls offset a weakness elsewhere, e.g. log review where segregation of duties is not possible.
cards.tip: Preventive is usually the BEST control; when it is not possible, look for a compensating detective control.

cards.title: General controls vs application controls
points: IT general controls (ITGC) cover the environment: access, change management, operations, backup.
Application controls work inside a system: input, processing and output controls.
Weak ITGCs mean application controls cannot be relied on.
cards.tip: Test ITGCs before relying on automated application controls.

cards.title: Fraud risk factors
points: Fraud triangle: pressure/incentive, opportunity, rationalisation.
Controls reduce opportunity: segregation of duties, approvals, monitoring, mandatory leave.

cards.title: Audit project management
points: Plan, staff and schedule the audit; monitor progress against the audit program.
Use skilled staff; supervise and review work papers.
Communicate early with auditee management to agree scope and timing.

cards.title: Compliance vs substantive testing
points: Compliance (test of controls) checks whether a control exists and operates as designed.
Substantive testing checks the integrity of actual data and transactions (balances, records).
Strong controls from compliance testing allow less substantive testing; weak controls require more.
cards.tip: Testing whether access is approved = compliance test. Recalculating balances = substantive test.

cards.title: Audit sampling
points: Statistical sampling uses probability to set size and evaluate results objectively; non-statistical (judgmental) relies on auditor judgment.
Attribute sampling estimates a rate of occurrence (compliance tests); variable sampling estimates a monetary value (substantive tests).
Stop-or-go sampling halts early when few errors are expected; discovery sampling looks for at least one instance (e.g. fraud).
Key terms: confidence coefficient, level of risk, precision, expected error rate, tolerable error, population standard deviation.
cards.tip: Higher confidence or lower tolerable error means a larger sample. A higher expected error rate also needs a larger sample.

cards.title: Audit evidence
points: Good evidence is sufficient, reliable, relevant and useful.
Most reliable: independent external sources, evidence obtained directly by the auditor, system-generated data.
Less reliable: verbal statements and evidence provided by the auditee.
Techniques: observation, inquiry, inspection, reperformance, CAATs, data analytics; protect evidence chain of custody.
cards.tip: Evidence the auditor obtains directly beats evidence handed over by management.

cards.title: Audit data analytics and CAATs
points: CAATs (e.g. generalized audit software) test whole populations, find exceptions and duplicates.
Continuous auditing gives near real-time assurance on high-volume automated processes.
Validate the completeness and integrity of extracted data before analysis.
cards.tip: For very large transaction volumes, CAATs/data analytics give the best coverage.

cards.title: Online (continuous) auditing techniques
points: SCARF/EAM: embedded audit modules collect selected transactions continuously.
Integrated test facility (ITF): dummy entity processed with live data; must be removed from results.
Snapshots record transaction paths; audit hooks flag suspicious transactions; CIS (continuous and intermittent simulation).
cards.tip: ITF risk: test data contaminating real results.

cards.title: Reporting and follow-up
points: Report findings with condition, criteria, cause, effect and recommendation; discuss with management first.
Management responds with action plans, owners and dates; the auditor follows up later.
The auditor may not suppress significant findings because management disagrees; include management’s response.
cards.tip: Before finalising a report, discuss findings with the auditee to confirm facts.

cards.title: Control self-assessment (CSA)
points: Management and staff assess their own controls, usually in facilitated workshops.
Benefits: early detection of risk, ownership of controls, better employee awareness.
CSA supplements, but does not replace, the internal audit function; the auditor acts as facilitator.
cards.tip: The objective of CSA is to make control monitoring a business responsibility.

cards.title: Laws, regulations and industry standards
points: Identify laws and regulations that affect the business (privacy, financial reporting, sector rules) and map them to controls.
Management owns compliance; the auditor checks that obligations are identified, owned and monitored.
Industry standards (PCI DSS, ISO 27001, NIST) may be contractual or voluntary.
cards.tip: First step in a compliance review: identify the applicable legal and regulatory requirements.

cards.title: COBIT (governance framework)
points: COBIT separates governance (evaluate, direct, monitor: board) from management (plan, build, run, monitor).
COBIT 2019 is current; it replaced COBIT 5 and adds design factors and focus areas.
Principles include meeting stakeholder needs, a holistic approach and a dynamic governance system.
Enablers/components: processes, structures, principles and policies, information, culture, people/skills, services/infrastructure/applications.
cards.tip: Your revision PDF still says COBIT 5. The current exam uses COBIT 2019 concepts.

cards.title: Corporate governance and GEIT
points: Corporate governance: the board sets direction and holds management accountable for performance and risk.
Governance of enterprise IT (GEIT) makes IT deliver value, manage risk and use resources in line with business goals.
Governance (board) evaluates, directs and monitors; management plans, builds, runs and monitors.
cards.tip: IT strategy must be derived from business strategy, not the other way round.

cards.title: Auditor’s role in IT governance
points: Assess whether governance structures align IT with business objectives and manage risk.
Review that roles, accountability and reporting to the board are clear.
Provide independent assurance; do not set strategy.

cards.title: IT strategy committee vs IT steering committee
points: IT strategy committee: board level; advises the board on IT strategy and alignment.
IT steering committee: executive level; prioritises projects, approves investments, monitors delivery and resources.
Steering committee members come from business and IT management.
cards.tip: Project prioritisation and approval of IT investment = steering committee.

cards.title: Information security roles and responsibilities
points: Board and senior management own security governance; the CISO manages the programme.
Data owners classify data and approve access; custodians implement controls; users follow policy.
Security administrators should be segregated from users and developers.
cards.tip: Data owners, not IT, are responsible for classifying data and authorizing access.

cards.title: Enterprise architecture (EA)
points: EA describes business, data, application and technology layers and how they fit together (e.g. Zachman, TOGAF).
It reduces duplication and complexity and guides investment decisions.
Auditors check that new projects comply with the target architecture and exceptions are approved.

cards.title: Enterprise risk management
points: Identify assets, threats and vulnerabilities; assess impact and likelihood; treat; monitor.
Risk appetite is set by senior management/board; risk owners accept residual risk.
Losses can be direct (money, assets) or indirect (reputation, legal, productivity).
cards.tip: Risk assessment must start with identifying and valuing information assets.

cards.title: Privacy vs confidentiality
points: Privacy concerns the rights of individuals over personal data (collection, use, consent, retention).
Confidentiality is protecting any information from unauthorized disclosure.
Privacy principles: notice, choice/consent, purpose limitation, minimisation, access, security, retention, accountability.
Auditor checks privacy impact assessments, legal compliance (e.g. GDPR) and controls over personal data.
cards.tip: A privacy impact assessment should be done early, when a system handling personal data is designed.

cards.title: Classification of information assets
points: Classify by sensitivity and criticality; the data owner decides the class.
Classification defines access rules, handling, retention and destruction.
Example levels: public, internal, confidential, restricted/secret.
cards.tip: Classification is the basis for choosing appropriate access controls.

cards.title: Human resource management
points: Hiring with background checks, signed confidentiality and acceptable-use agreements.
Training, mandatory leave and job rotation help detect fraud.
Termination: revoke access immediately, recover assets, conduct exit procedures.
cards.tip: Mandatory vacation / job rotation are detective controls against fraud.

cards.title: Sourcing and outsourcing
points: Options: insourced, outsourced, hybrid; onsite, offsite, offshore.
Accountability stays with the organisation; outsource the activity, not the responsibility.
Contracts need SLAs, right-to-audit, security, confidentiality, exit and data return clauses.
Offshore risks: legal/jurisdiction, privacy, communication and continuity.
cards.tip: Right-to-audit clause and SLA monitoring are key controls for outsourced services.

cards.title: IT balanced scorecard
points: Measures IT across four perspectives: business contribution, user orientation, operational excellence and future orientation.
Links IT performance to business goals using leading and lagging indicators.
Prerequisite: defined key performance indicators that matter to the business.
cards.tip: The BSC is a management/performance tool, not a risk assessment tool.

cards.title: Maturity and process improvement models
points: Capability/maturity models (e.g. CMMI) measure process maturity from initial/ad hoc to optimized.
IDEAL model for improvement: Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning.
Used to set a target maturity and plan improvement steps.

cards.title: Quality assurance
points: QA ensures that staff follow standards and processes; quality control tests the product.
QA function should be independent of development.

cards.title: Portfolio and program management
points: Portfolio management selects and prioritises the right projects for the strategy and optimises resources.
A program is a group of related projects managed together to deliver a common outcome.
Projects have defined start/end, scope, budget and deliverables.

cards.title: Project organisation forms
points: Functional (influence) structure: project manager has little authority.
Pure project: project manager has full authority over the team.
Matrix: authority shared between functional and project managers.

cards.title: Project roles
points: Senior management/sponsor provides funding and is accountable for success; steering committee gives direction.
Project manager runs day-to-day delivery; user management owns requirements and acceptance; QA verifies quality.
Security officer ensures security controls are designed in.
cards.tip: The project sponsor owns the business case and approves funding.

cards.title: Planning tools: WBS, OBS, estimating
points: Work breakdown structure (WBS) splits the project into manageable work packages; OBS shows who is responsible.
Estimating: analogous, parametric, bottom-up, and actual costs. Function point analysis sizes software by functionality.
PERT uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic estimates: (O + 4M + P) / 6.
Critical path = longest path with zero slack; Gantt charts show schedule; earned value compares planned, earned and actual cost.
cards.tip: Function point analysis is the BEST way to estimate size of business software early.

cards.title: Executing, controlling and closing
points: Control scope changes through formal change requests; manage resources and risks continuously.
Risk process: identify, assess, manage, monitor, evaluate the risk process.
Closing: formal acceptance, lessons learned, release resources, archive documentation.
cards.tip: Uncontrolled scope change (scope creep) is a leading cause of project failure.

cards.title: Benefits realization and business case
points: The business case justifies an investment: benefits, costs, risks, alternatives and alignment with strategy.
Revisit the business case at each major phase gate; stop the project if it is no longer viable.
Benefits realization continues after go-live and is measured against the business case.
cards.tip: The business case should be reviewed throughout the project, not only at approval.

cards.title: Traditional SDLC (waterfall)
points: Phases: feasibility, requirements, design, build, test, implementation, post-implementation review.
Each phase has deliverables and sign-off before the next; good for stable, well-understood requirements.
Requirements errors found late are the most expensive to fix.
cards.tip: User involvement in requirements definition is the most important success factor.

cards.title: Agile, prototyping and re-engineering
points: Agile delivers small increments in short iterations (sprints) with close user involvement; less documentation.
Prototyping quickly shows users a working model; risk: weak controls and scope growth.
Re-engineering updates an existing system; reverse engineering analyses a system to learn its design.
cards.tip: In agile, controls and documentation still matter; the auditor checks they are built into the process.

cards.title: AI and expert systems
points: Expert systems use a knowledge base (rules, decision trees, semantic nets), inference engine and explanation module.
Risks: incorrect or outdated rules, poor validation of decisions, lack of explainability.
Auditors check how knowledge is validated and changes to rules are controlled.

cards.title: Input controls and data validation edits
points: Sequence check (no gaps/duplicates in numbering), limit check (upper bound), range check (between limits).
Validity check (allowed values), reasonableness check (sensible against norms), existence check (data entered correctly against criteria).
Key verification (re-keyed by a second person), check digit (detects transcription errors), completeness check (no missing fields).
Duplicate check (no repeated transactions) and logical relationship check (fields consistent with each other).
cards.tip: Check digit = detects transposition and transcription errors at input.

cards.title: Processing and output controls
points: Processing: run-to-run totals, control totals, reconciliation, limit checks on calculated amounts, exception reports.
Output: distribution lists, report balancing, secure storage of sensitive forms, retention rules.
Batch controls: record counts, financial totals, hash totals.
cards.tip: Hash totals are meaningless sums used only to detect missing or altered records.

cards.title: Data integrity testing and ACID
points: Relational integrity tests check data within a table; referential integrity tests check relationships between tables (foreign keys).
Online transaction processing relies on ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
cards.tip: Atomicity = all or nothing; a failed transaction is fully rolled back.

cards.title: Test approaches and test classification
points: Bottom-up testing starts with modules; top-down starts with interfaces and finds interface errors early.
Unit, interface/integration, system (recovery, security, load, volume, stress, performance) and final acceptance testing.
QA testing checks technical quality; user acceptance testing (UAT) checks business requirements and is signed off by users.
Other tests: alpha/beta, pilot, white-box/black-box, regression, parallel, sociability.
cards.tip: Regression testing ensures changes did not break existing functionality.

cards.title: Certification and accreditation
points: Certification is the technical evaluation of a system’s controls against requirements.
Accreditation is management’s formal acceptance of the residual risk and authorization to operate.

cards.title: Implementation configuration and release management
points: Configuration management keeps baselines of approved system settings in a CMDB.
Releases are planned, tested, approved and deployed with rollback plans.
Production access for developers is restricted; migration done by an independent function.
cards.tip: Version control and configuration baselines prevent unauthorized changes reaching production.

cards.title: Changeover (go-live) techniques
points: Parallel changeover: old and new run together; safest but costly.
Phased changeover: modules introduced in stages.
Abrupt (direct cut-over): fastest, highest risk; needs a fallback plan.
cards.tip: Data conversion controls (record counts, control totals) are critical at changeover.

cards.title: Post-implementation review and benchmarking
points: PIR checks whether objectives and benefits were achieved and identifies lessons learned.
Benchmarking compares processes with best performers: plan, research, observe, analyse, adapt, improve.
cards.tip: A PIR is done after the system has stabilised, typically several months after go-live.

cards.title: IS operations and IT service management
points: IS operations run, monitor and support systems: job scheduling, monitoring, incident handling, backups.
ITSM frameworks: ITIL (service lifecycle/value system) and ISO/IEC 20000-1 (certifiable service management standard).
Management should monitor operations with performance reports, logs and exception reports.
cards.tip: Your PDF cites ISO 20000-1:2011; the current version is ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018.

cards.title: Networks: OSI and LAN/WAN
points: OSI layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application.
LAN media: twisted pair (cheap, interference), fibre (secure, fast, hard to tap), wireless (convenient, needs encryption).
Devices: hubs (L1), switches/bridges (L2), routers (L3), gateways (higher layers).
WAN: leased lines, packet switching, MPLS, VPN (remote access, intranet, extranet).
cards.tip: Fibre optic is the most secure medium against eavesdropping.

cards.title: SLA, OLA and service monitoring
points: SLA: agreement between IT/provider and the business on service levels and measures.
OLA: internal agreement between IT groups that supports the SLA.
Monitoring tools: exception reports, system and application logs, availability and performance reports.
cards.tip: SLA reports must be based on measured data, not provider self-statements.

cards.title: Database management (DBMS)
points: DBMS architecture: external, conceptual and internal schemas; metadata held in a data dictionary/directory.
Models: hierarchical, network and relational (tables, keys, normalization to reduce redundancy).
Controls: access via DBMS only, referential integrity, backup and recovery, logging of changes, DBA activity review.
cards.tip: The DBA’s activities should be logged and reviewed by someone independent.

cards.title: IT asset management
points: Maintain a complete, accurate inventory of hardware, software and licences, with owners.
Asset lifecycle: acquire, deploy, maintain, retire and securely dispose (data sanitisation).
An accurate inventory is the foundation for risk assessment, patching and licensing compliance.
cards.tip: You cannot protect assets you do not know you have.

cards.title: Job scheduling and production automation
points: Scheduling software runs batch jobs in the right order with dependencies and restart points.
Controls: approved schedules, restricted changes to job definitions, review of job logs and exceptions.
Reduces operator errors compared to manual job initiation.
cards.tip: Changes to production job schedules need the same change control as program changes.

cards.title: System interfaces
points: Interfaces move data between systems (APIs, file transfers, messaging).
Controls: reconciliation of record counts/totals, error handling and alerts, encryption in transit, ownership of each interface.
Undocumented interfaces are a common audit finding.
cards.tip: Reconcile source and target totals to confirm complete, accurate transfer.

cards.title: 4.5 Shadow IT (emphasised in the new syllabus)
points: Systems, software, cloud services or hardware used without approval from IT or security.
Risks: unvetted tools, security vulnerabilities, data leakage and loss of data control, non-compliance.
Controls: shadow IT policy (approve before use); IT as a service-delivery partner; IT review of all technology purchases; consolidate platforms.
Also: restrict admin rights and software installation; user education; monitor user activity and network traffic for unapproved tools (e.g. CASB).
cards.tip: Example: a marketing team adopts an unapproved cloud project tool. Best response: policy plus IT working with the team to provide an approved, secure alternative.

cards.title: Network performance and management
points: Metrics: latency, throughput, availability, error rates, utilisation.
Tools: network performance monitors, protocol analysers, SNMP, help desk reports.
Capacity planning prevents performance problems as demand grows.

cards.title: Incident vs problem management
points: Incident management restores normal service as quickly as possible.
Problem management finds and removes the root cause of one or more incidents to prevent recurrence.
Known errors are documented with workarounds until fixed.
cards.tip: Root cause = problem management.

cards.title: Help desk / support
points: Logs every incident, prioritises, resolves or escalates, and tracks to closure.
Trend analysis of tickets feeds problem management.

cards.title: Change, patch and release management
points: Change management: request, impact assessment, approval, testing, scheduled implementation, post-change review.
Emergency changes are allowed but must be documented and approved after the fact.
Patch management: inventory, assess, test, deploy, verify; prioritise by risk.
Release management groups approved changes into planned releases; segregate development, test and production.
cards.tip: Developers must not migrate their own code to production.

cards.title: NEW 4.9: Operational log management
points: Operational logs (audit trails) record system events, user actions and changes in day-to-day IT operations.
A log record should capture: type of event, time, location, source (who/what triggered it), outcome and identity of parties involved.
Purposes: monitoring and investigation, accountability, and a compensating control where small teams cannot segregate duties.
cards.tip: Log review is a classic compensating control when segregation of duties is not possible.

cards.title: NEW 4.9.1: Types of logs
points: Event log (logins, failed passwords, network/app events); server log; system log (OS start-up, errors, shutdowns).
Access log (who accessed which file or app); change log (chronological changes); availability log (uptime vs SLA).
Threat log (traffic matching a security profile); database log (inserts, updates, deletes); error log; firewall log (traffic allowed/blocked).
cards.tip: Availability logs are the evidence for SLA uptime reporting.

cards.title: NEW 4.9.2: Log management cycle
points: 1 Collect data from servers, network devices and applications; 2 generate alerts on suspicious activity.
3 Store logs centrally (log server or SIEM); 4 analyse stored data for issues alerts missed.
5 Report concerns to the right teams; 6 implement action plans (contain, remediate, patch, update rules).
Infrastructure: log generation (hosts), log analysis and storage (log servers), log monitoring (real-time, e.g. SIEM rules and thresholds).

cards.title: Securing logs
points: Intruders try to alter or delete logs to hide activity; logs must be protected so they remain authentic evidence.
Centralize logs on a secure server/SIEM, restrict access, protect integrity (write-once, hashing) and synchronise time sources.
Define retention to meet legal and investigation needs.
cards.tip: Best protection for audit trails: send them to a separate, secured central log server that administrators of the source system cannot change.

cards.title: Business impact analysis (BIA)
points: Identifies critical processes, impact of disruption over time, and recovery requirements (RTO, RPO).
Approaches: questionnaires, interviews with key users, workshops.
Results drive classification of systems and the recovery strategy.
cards.tip: Input from business process owners is the most important source for a BIA.

cards.title: Classifying systems by criticality
points: Critical: cannot be replaced by manual methods; very low tolerance.
Vital: can be done manually for a short time.
Sensitive: manual for a tolerable period at higher cost.
Non-critical: can be interrupted for a long time at little cost.

cards.title: RPO, RTO and related parameters
points: RPO: maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time back from the incident; drives backup frequency.
RTO: maximum acceptable downtime; drives the recovery strategy.
Lower RTO/RPO means higher cost. Other parameters: interruption window, service delivery objective, maximum tolerable outage.
cards.tip: Low RPO -> frequent backups or mirroring. Low RTO -> hot site or high availability.

cards.title: Recovery strategies and sites
points: Hot site: fully equipped, ready in hours. Warm site: partly equipped. Cold site: space and utilities only.
Mirrored/duplicate sites, mobile sites and reciprocal agreements (hard to enforce).
Choice depends on criticality, RTO/RPO and cost.
cards.tip: Reciprocal agreements are the least reliable recovery option.

cards.title: Backup and restoration
points: Full, incremental (changes since last backup of any type) and differential (changes since last full) backups.
Rotation schemes such as grandfather-father-son; store copies offsite and test restores.
Restore requires the last full plus all incrementals, or the last full plus the latest differential.
cards.tip: Backups that are never test-restored give no assurance.

cards.title: Business continuity planning (BCP)
points: Lifecycle: policy, BIA, strategy, plan development, training, testing, maintenance.
The BCP covers people, processes and business functions; DRP covers IT recovery.
Senior management approves and is ultimately responsible for the BCP.
cards.tip: The first step in BCP is the business impact analysis.

cards.title: BCP plan testing
points: Checklist review, structured walk-through/table-top, simulation, parallel test, full interruption test.
Paper tests first; full interruption tests carry the highest risk and are done rarely.
Every test needs objectives, results measured against them and lessons learned.
cards.tip: Parallel test = recovery site processes live data alongside production without disrupting it.

cards.title: Disaster recovery planning (DRP)
points: DRP restores IT systems after a disaster; the BCP keeps the whole business running.
DRP is driven by the BIA: recovery priorities, RTO and RPO.

cards.title: Recovery teams
points: Incident response, emergency action, damage assessment, offsite storage, software, application, network, user and relocation teams.
Each team has clear responsibilities and contact lists kept current.

cards.title: DR testing methods
points: Checklist, walk-through, simulation, parallel and full interruption tests.
Test results are compared with objectives; failures feed plan updates.

cards.title: ISMS and security management
points: An ISMS (ISO/IEC 27001) is a management system to establish, implement, maintain and improve information security.
Key elements: senior management commitment, policies and procedures, organisation, awareness, monitoring and compliance, incident handling.
ISO 27000 family: 27001 requirements (certifiable), 27002 controls guidance, 27005 risk management.
cards.tip: Senior management commitment is the most critical success factor for information security.

cards.title: Security control design
points: Categories: managerial/administrative, technical/logical, physical.
Functions: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, recovery, compensating.

cards.title: Environmental exposures and controls
points: Power problems: blackout (total failure), brownout (reduced voltage), sags, spikes, surges, electromagnetic interference.
Controls: UPS and generators, surge protectors and line conditioners, alarm panels, water detectors, fire/smoke detectors, extinguishers.
Fire suppression: dry-pipe/pre-action sprinklers and clean-agent gas systems (e.g. FM-200) for data centres; halon is banned.
Raised floors, humidity/temperature control, fire-resistant materials, regular inspections, emergency power-off switch.
cards.tip: Dry-pipe sprinklers reduce risk of water leaks; test fire systems regularly.

cards.title: Physical access exposures and controls
points: Exposures: unauthorized entry, tailgating/piggybacking, theft, damage, viewing sensitive data.
Controls: badges/smart cards, biometric locks, mantraps/deadman doors, guards, CCTV, visitor logs and escorts.
Keep data centres in low-profile locations; review access lists and logs regularly.
cards.tip: Mantrap (deadman door) is the best control against piggybacking.

cards.title: Access control models
points: Physical access controls protect facilities; logical access controls protect systems and data.
Mandatory access control (MAC): system-enforced labels; users cannot change. Discretionary (DAC): owner grants access.
Role-based access control (RBAC) assigns rights to roles; least privilege and need-to-know apply.
cards.tip: MAC is stricter than DAC because users cannot pass on rights.

cards.title: Identification and authentication
points: Identification = who you claim to be; authentication = proof; authorization = what you can do.
Factors: something you know, something you have, something you are/do. Multi-factor uses two or more different types.
Weaknesses: weak or shared passwords, no lockout, credentials sent in clear text.
cards.tip: Two passwords is still single-factor; MFA requires different factor types.

cards.title: Biometrics
points: Process: enrolment, then a sensor captures, quality is assessed, features are compared, decision is made.
Physical: palm, hand geometry, iris, retina, fingerprint, face. Behavioural: signature, voice, keystroke.
FRR (false rejection, type I) inconveniences users; FAR (false acceptance, type II) is the security risk.
Equal error rate (EER/CER) where FAR = FRR: lower is better.
cards.tip: For high security, focus on a low FAR. To compare devices, use the EER.

cards.title: Single sign-on (SSO)
points: One authentication gives access to many systems; improves usability and administration.
Risk: a single compromised credential exposes everything; single point of failure.
Mitigate with strong authentication (MFA) on the SSO.

cards.title: Firewalls
points: Packet filter: checks addresses/ports; fast but simple, vulnerable to spoofing.
Application-level (proxy) firewall: inspects application data; circuit-level: controls sessions.
Stateful inspection: tracks connection state; more secure than packet filters.
Architectures: screened host, dual-homed host, screened subnet (DMZ) - the DMZ is the most secure.
cards.tip: Application-level gateways give the most granular control; DMZ isolates public-facing servers.

cards.title: Data loss prevention (DLP)
points: DLP discovers, monitors and blocks sensitive data at rest, in motion and in use.
Depends on good data classification and well-tuned policies.
Alerts need a defined response process.
cards.tip: Data classification must come before DLP rules can be effective.

cards.title: Cryptography and encryption
points: Symmetric (one shared key, e.g. AES): fast; problem is key distribution.
Asymmetric (public/private key pair, e.g. RSA, ECC): solves key exchange; slower.
Hashing (SHA-2) gives integrity; digital signatures (hash signed with sender’s private key) give integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.
Encrypt with recipient’s public key for confidentiality.
cards.tip: Non-repudiation comes from the sender’s private key; confidentiality from the recipient’s public key.

cards.title: PKI and digital certificates
points: Certificate authority (CA) issues and signs certificates binding a public key to an identity; RA verifies identity.
Certificate revocation list (CRL) / OCSP show revoked certificates.
Protect the CA’s private key above everything else.

cards.title: Cloud and virtualized environments
points: Shared responsibility: provider secures the cloud; customer secures configuration, identities and data (varies by IaaS/PaaS/SaaS).
Assurance: SOC 2 / ISO 27001 reports, right-to-audit, data location, exit and encryption key management.
Virtualization risks: hypervisor compromise, VM sprawl, weak isolation; harden and patch the hypervisor.
cards.tip: The customer remains accountable for its data in the cloud.

cards.title: Mobile, wireless and IoT devices
points: Mobile: mobile device management (MDM), encryption, remote wipe, app control, BYOD policy.
Wireless: WPA3/WPA2-Enterprise, strong authentication, disable WPS, detect rogue access points.
IoT: change default passwords, patch firmware, segment IoT networks.
cards.tip: Remote wipe and encryption are key controls for lost mobile devices.

cards.title: Security awareness and HR security
points: Awareness programmes are continuous, role-based and measured.
Before employment: screening/background checks; during: policies, training, disciplinary process; termination: remove access, return assets.
cards.tip: The most effective control against social engineering is user awareness.

cards.title: Computer crime and attack methods
points: Perpetrators: insiders (biggest risk), former employees, hackers, crackers, organised crime, nation states.
Attacks: botnets, brute force, war dialing/driving/chalking, eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle, masquerading, pharming, piggybacking.
Salami (small amounts skimmed), logic bomb (if-then trigger), denial of service (e.g. ping of death), traffic analysis (passive).
Phishing and social engineering target people rather than technology.
cards.tip: Passive attacks (eavesdropping, traffic analysis) are hard to detect; encryption is the best control.

cards.title: IDS, IPS, honeypots and honeynets
points: IDS detects and alerts: network-based or host-based; signature-based, statistical/anomaly-based or neural network.
IDS cannot fix weak policy, authentication or application flaws, and needs tuning to reduce false positives.
IPS sits in-line and blocks attacks automatically (risk: blocking legitimate traffic).
Honeypots/honeynets are decoys to study attackers: high-interaction or low-interaction.
cards.tip: Anomaly-based IDS can detect new attacks but produces more false positives.

cards.title: Security monitoring logs, tools and techniques
points: SIEM collects and correlates logs from many sources and alerts on suspicious patterns.
Monitoring needs defined use cases, tuned thresholds and a response process; protect log integrity.
Related to 4A9 Operational log management; see those notes.

cards.title: Incident response phases
points: Preparation, identification/detection, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.
Preserve evidence during response; escalate per plan.
cards.tip: Containment comes before eradication.

cards.title: Evidence collection and forensics
points: Preserve evidence: identify, collect, preserve, analyse, present; keep chain of custody.
Work on bit-for-bit forensic images, verified with hash values; never on the original.
Involve legal counsel and law enforcement as appropriate.
cards.tip: Chain of custody is essential for evidence to be admissible.
